title: Anti-D immunoglobulin
what: This is an injection for a woman with Rh-negative blood. It protects the baby from Rh disease in this and future pregnancies.
why: If the mother is Rh-negative and the baby may be Rh-positive. Usually around 28 weeks, after birth, and at other times as your doctor decides.
duration: the injection takes 1 to 2 minutes; afterward you are watched for about 30 minutes
tell_doctor: Your Rh type, and your partner's if known
If you had anti-D injections before
If you had bleeding or an injury to your belly
If antibodies were found in your blood test

prepare.title: Test
prepare.text: Your blood is usually checked for antibodies before the injection.

prepare.title: Food
prepare.text: No special prep is usually needed. Eat as usual.

prepare.title: Clothes
prepare.text: Wear comfortable clothes. The injection is usually in the upper arm or buttock.

steps: The doctor checks your tests and how far along you are
The nurse confirms your name and the medicine
The injection is given into a muscle
You stay at the clinic for half an hour to be watched
The date of the injection is noted in your pregnancy record
feel: The injection site may be a little sore for a day or two
after: After the injection, your antibody test may sometimes become positive. This is expected
After birth, your baby's blood is checked for Rh type
If your baby is Rh-positive, you usually get another injection within 72 hours
red_flags: A rash, a swollen face, or trouble breathing: call emergency services
Bleeding or belly pain during pregnancy

faq.q: Why get the injection in a first pregnancy?
faq.a: It protects both this pregnancy and future ones. The risk is already there in the first pregnancy.

faq.q: Is the injection dangerous for my baby?
faq.a: Usually not. It is given to protect your baby.

reminders.text: Anti-D injection tomorrow. Bring your pregnancy record.
